passage.bullet: Philip II married the Molossian princess Olympias around 357 BC → cemented a strategic military alliance with neighbouring Epirus
Macedonian kings practised royal polygamy with no fixed rule of eldest-son succession → every marriage created potential rival heirs
Surrounded by rival factions at Pella, Olympias fought relentlessly to protect young Alexander’s political claim → shaped his court alertness from birth

context.bullet: Philip II’s eighteen-foot sarissa phalanx and Mount Pangaeum gold mines turned Macedon into Greece’s dominant military state → set a high bar for his son

stems.stem: King Philip II married the Molossian princess ____________ in order to secure a strategic border alliance with...

lesson_1_1.watch_out: Olympias was a royal Greek-speaking Molossian princess from Epirus— yet pure-blooded Macedonian nobles like Attalus still treated her as a foreign outsider.

passage.bullet: Olympias taught Alexander that her Epirote house descended from Achilles while Philip claimed Heracles → gave Alexander warrior role models to surpass
Olympias led ecstatic Orphic and Dionysian rites with tame serpents and dreamed a thunderbolt struck her womb → encouraged belief in divine conception
Plutarch records Philip seeing a giant serpent beside sleeping Olympias and Delphi urging worship of Ammon → planted rumours that Zeus Ammon fathered Alexander

context.bullet: On Alexander’s birth day in July 356 BC the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus burned down while Philip’s horse won at Olympia → read by seers as portents of invincibility

stems.stem: Through Olympias’ Molossian ancestry, young Alexander believed he descended directly from the Trojan War hero ____________...

lesson_1_1.watch_out: Plutarch wrote over four centuries later as a moral biographer—treat the thunderbolt and lion-seal dreams as retrospective portents rather than literal diary facts.

passage.bullet: While Philip’s grooms failed to mount thirteen-talent Bucephalas, Alexander observed the stallion feared its own shadow → turned its bridle towards the sun
Philip II wept with joy and declared Macedonia was too small for Alexander → showed genuine paternal pride in his son’s nerve and intelligence
Whenever Philip captured a city, Alexander complained his father would leave nothing brilliant left to achieve → exposed intense competitive rivalry

context.bullet: Bucephalas carried Alexander across Asia from Macedon to India until 326 BC → became a living symbol of his heroic leadership

lesson_1_1.watch_out: Avoid claiming Alexander and Philip hated each other throughout his childhood—Plutarch shows deep mutual pride alongside fierce competition for glory.

passage.bullet: In 337 BC Philip II married Cleopatra Eurydice, young Macedonian niece of General Attalus → threatened Olympias’ and Alexander’s court standing
Attalus urged banquet guests to pray to the gods for a legitimate heir to the throne → implied half-Molossian Alexander was illegitimate
Alexander hurled his cup, Philip drew his sword and tripped drunkenly between couches, and Alexander mocked him → Olympias fled to Epirus and Alexander to Illyria

context.bullet: The insult stung doubly because Alexander had already studied under Aristotle at Mieza, subdued the Maedi as regent, and broken the Sacred Band at Chaeronea in 338 BC

lesson_1_1.watch_out: Distinguish Cleopatra Eurydice—Philip II’s young Macedonian bride in 337 BC—from Queen Cleopatra VII of Egypt three centuries later!

passage.bullet: King Lysimachus stamped the obverse with Alexander wearing the curved ram’s horn of Zeus Ammon → broadcast Alexander’s status as son of a god
Alexander wears the royal cloth diadem with upward divine gaze → linked absolute Asian kingship with superhuman charisma
The reverse depicts seated Athena holding winged Nike crowning Lysimachus’ Greek name → transferred Alexander’s invincibility onto his former bodyguard’s kingdom

context.bullet: Minted around 305 to 281 BC within a generation of Alexander’s death → corroborates how rapidly Olympias’ and Siwah’s divine myth became state currency

lesson_1_1.watch_out: Examiner Report Alert: The curved horn on Lysimachus’ coin is the ram’s horn of Zeus Ammon—NEVER confuse it with the Egyptian god Ptah!
